questions.question: On which planet does it rain diamonds?
questions.fun_fact: On Neptune and Uranus, immense pressure breaks methane apart. The carbon crystallises into diamonds that fall through the atmosphere — some thought to be hailstone-sized.

questions.question: How does a Venusian day compare to a Venusian year?

answers.text: The day is longer than the year

questions.fun_fact: Venus rotates so slowly that one Venus day (243 Earth days) lasts longer than one Venus year (225 Earth days). It also spins backwards relative to most planets.

questions.question: What would happen to your blood in space without a suit?

answers.text: It would neither boil nor freeze

questions.fun_fact: Common misconception: blood does NOT boil in vacuum because your blood vessels maintain enough internal pressure. You'd pass out in about 15 seconds, but your blood stays liquid.

questions.question: What is the largest known volcano in the solar system?
questions.fun_fact: Olympus Mons rises about 22 km — nearly three times the height of Mount Everest — and its base is the size of the state of Arizona.

questions.question: What colour is the sunset on Mars?
questions.fun_fact: Mars has red daytime skies but blue sunsets. The fine dust scatters red light forward and lets blue light pass through near the sun — exactly opposite to Earth.

questions.question: What happens if you try to fall into a black hole feet-first?

answers.text: You get stretched into a thin string
You bounce off the event horizon

questions.fun_fact: Physicists call it 'spaghettification': gravity pulls your feet much harder than your head, stretching you into a long thin shape long before you reach the singularity.

questions.question: Which is the only moon in the solar system with a thick atmosphere?
questions.fun_fact: Saturn's moon Titan has an atmosphere denser than Earth's, with lakes and rivers of liquid methane. It is the only place besides Earth with stable surface liquid.

questions.question: What is the temperature on Mercury's night side?
questions.fun_fact: Despite being the closest planet to the Sun, Mercury has almost no atmosphere to retain heat. Day-side temperatures hit 430°C, but the night side plunges to about -170°C.

questions.question: What would a teaspoon of neutron star material weigh on Earth?
questions.fun_fact: Neutron stars cram more mass than the Sun into a ball about 20 km across. A single sugar-cube of the stuff would weigh roughly as much as Mount Everest.

questions.question: Where in the solar system does it most likely snow metal?
questions.fun_fact: Venus's highest peaks are coated in a reflective 'frost' thought to be metallic compounds like bismuth or lead sulphide that condense out of the scorching atmosphere at altitude.

questions.question: If you fell into a perfectly frictionless tunnel through Earth, how long would the trip to the other side take?
questions.fun_fact: Ignoring air and friction, gravity pulls you in simple harmonic motion. Any straight tunnel through Earth — pole to pole or otherwise — takes the same roughly 42 minutes.

questions.question: Does time pass faster at the top of a mountain or at sea level?
questions.fun_fact: General relativity: clocks tick faster where gravity is weaker. Your head ages very slightly faster than your feet — measurable with modern atomic clocks.

questions.question: Can a single photon be in two places at once?
questions.fun_fact: In quantum mechanics, particles exist in superposition until measured. The double-slit experiment shows a single photon interfering with itself, as if it took both paths.

questions.question: What happens to glass over many centuries — does it slowly flow like a liquid?
questions.fun_fact: The old 'medieval window panes are thicker at the bottom because glass flows' story is a myth. Glass is an amorphous solid — the thickness was just how it was made.

questions.question: What happens to the boiling point of water at the top of Mount Everest?
questions.fun_fact: Lower air pressure means water boils sooner. At Everest's summit it boils at around 70°C — too cool to properly cook food or sterilise water.

questions.question: Why is the sky blue?

answers.text: Air molecules scatter blue light more than red
The atmosphere is made of a blue gas

questions.fun_fact: Rayleigh scattering: shorter (bluer) wavelengths bounce off air molecules much more than longer (redder) ones. At sunset, light travels through more air so most blue is scattered away.

questions.question: If you could hear sound in space, how loud would the Sun be on Earth?

answers.text: About as loud as a jet engine

questions.fun_fact: The Sun's surface pulses constantly. If space carried sound, the noise reaching Earth would be roughly 100 decibels — like standing near a jet at takeoff.

questions.question: What does it feel like to touch absolute zero?

answers.text: Impossible — you can never actually reach it

questions.fun_fact: The third law of thermodynamics says you can get arbitrarily close to absolute zero (-273.15°C) but never actually reach it. Labs have hit a few billionths of a degree above.

questions.question: What is the only force that gets stronger as objects move apart?

answers.text: The strong nuclear force between quarks

questions.fun_fact: Quarks are bound by gluons in a way that grows stronger with distance — like a rubber band. That's why you can never isolate a single quark.

questions.question: Why does a helium balloon make your voice sound high?

answers.text: Helium changes the pitch your vocal cords vibrate at

questions.fun_fact: Your vocal cords vibrate at the same frequency, but sound travels nearly three times faster in helium. That shifts the resonance of your vocal tract upward, changing the timbre.

questions.question: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
questions.fun_fact: Mercury melts at -39°C, making it the only metal liquid at typical room temperature. Gallium melts in your hand (29°C) but is solid in a cool room.

questions.question: What happens when you drop a piece of caesium into water?
questions.fun_fact: Alkali metals get more reactive as you go down the group. Caesium reacts with water so fast that the hydrogen released ignites instantly — even ice triggers an explosion.

questions.question: Which element makes up about 75% of all visible matter in the universe?
questions.fun_fact: Most matter formed in the first minutes after the Big Bang was hydrogen. Heavier elements like oxygen and iron were forged later inside stars.

questions.question: Which substance expands when it freezes — making it unusual among materials?
questions.fun_fact: Almost all substances contract when they solidify, but water expands by about 9% — which is why ice floats and burst pipes are a winter hazard.

questions.question: Why is glass transparent to visible light but not to ultraviolet?

answers.text: Its electrons absorb UV photons but not visible ones
Glass has tiny holes that block UV
UV light is too small to fit through glass

questions.fun_fact: Visible light photons don't have enough energy to excite the electrons in silica glass, so they pass through. UV photons do — they get absorbed, which is why window glass blocks sunburn UVB.

questions.question: What's unusual about the noble gas helium at extremely low temperatures?

answers.text: It becomes a superfluid that climbs walls

questions.fun_fact: Below 2.17 K, helium-4 becomes a superfluid with zero viscosity. It can flow through tiny pores, form a thin creeping film, and even siphon itself out of an open container.

questions.question: Which acid is strong enough to dissolve glass?
questions.fun_fact: Hydrofluoric acid is actually a weak acid by pH, but it reacts with silicon dioxide. It's stored in plastic bottles because it would eat through glass containers.

questions.question: What's odd about the density of ordinary tap water at 4°C?

answers.text: Water is densest at 4°C, not at 0°C
Density of water doesn't change with temperature

questions.fun_fact: Water reaches maximum density at about 4°C. That's why lakes freeze top-down: the densest water sinks, leaving colder water and then ice floating on the surface — keeping fish alive below.

questions.question: Why does cutting an onion make you cry?

answers.text: It releases a gas that turns into mild sulphuric acid in your eyes
The smell triggers a reflex tear

questions.fun_fact: Damaged onion cells release an enzyme that produces syn-propanethial-S-oxide. The volatile gas reacts with the moisture in your eyes to form a tiny amount of sulphuric acid.

questions.question: What happens to a rubber band when you stretch it quickly?
questions.fun_fact: Counter-intuitively, rubber heats up when stretched and cools when released — opposite to most materials. Touch a thick rubber band to your lip while stretching it to feel the warmth.

questions.question: Which household device was invented after a chocolate bar melted in an engineer's pocket?
questions.fun_fact: In 1945 Percy Spencer noticed a chocolate bar melt while he stood near a radar magnetron. He tested popcorn, then an egg (which exploded), and patented the microwave oven.

questions.question: Which medicine was discovered after a scientist returned from holiday to a mouldy lab dish?
questions.fun_fact: Alexander Fleming came back in 1928 to find a Petri dish contaminated with Penicillium mould — and the bacteria around it dead. The discovery launched the antibiotic era.

questions.question: What did the inventor of Velcro get the idea from?

answers.text: Burrs sticking to his dog's fur

questions.fun_fact: Swiss engineer George de Mestral examined burrs under a microscope after a 1941 hike, saw their tiny hooks, and spent years recreating the design with synthetic fibres.

questions.question: Which everyday product was originally invented to clean soot off wallpaper?
questions.fun_fact: Play-Doh started as a 1930s wallpaper cleaner. When coal heating declined and vinyl wallpaper arrived, the company rebranded the malleable putty as a children's toy.

questions.question: Post-it Notes were created because of which lab accident?

answers.text: A scientist made a glue that wasn't sticky enough
A scientist spilled glue on a notebook
A scientist mixed two glues by mistake

questions.fun_fact: 3M's Spencer Silver invented a weak, reusable adhesive in 1968. It sat unused for years until a colleague used it to anchor bookmarks in his church hymnal — the Post-it was born.

questions.question: How was the artificial sweetener saccharin discovered?

answers.text: A chemist forgot to wash his hands and noticed dinner tasted sweet
A chemist tested cane sugar derivatives systematically

questions.fun_fact: In 1879 Constantin Fahlberg ate bread at home, noticed it was sweet, and traced the taste to a compound he'd handled in the lab — the world's first artificial sweetener.

questions.question: Safety glass was invented after a chemist did what?

answers.text: Dropped a coated flask and saw it cracked but didn't shatter
Heated sand to a new temperature
Melted plastic onto a window pane

questions.fun_fact: Édouard Bénédictus dropped a flask coated with dried cellulose nitrate in 1903 and noticed it held its shape. He patented laminated safety glass — now used in car windshields.

questions.question: What is the origin story of the Slinky toy?

answers.text: A naval engineer knocked a tension spring off a shelf
A child stretched out a Christmas decoration
A clockmaker built a faulty mechanism

questions.fun_fact: In 1943, Richard James was developing springs to stabilise ship instruments. One fell off a shelf and 'walked' down to the floor. His wife found the name 'Slinky' in a dictionary.

questions.question: How did the inventor of the pacemaker come to install one in himself?

answers.text: He miscalculated a resistor by a factor of 100
He used a clock spring as a model

questions.fun_fact: Wilson Greatbatch grabbed the wrong-value resistor in 1956 and built a circuit that pulsed like a heart. The implantable pacemaker that followed has saved millions of lives.

questions.question: Super Glue was discovered while researchers were trying to make what?

answers.text: Clear plastic gun sights for World War II

questions.fun_fact: Harry Coover stumbled on cyanoacrylate in 1942 while developing transparent plastic sights. It stuck to everything and was rejected — until he revisited it years later as adhesive.

questions.question: How many bones is a baby born with compared to an adult?
questions.fun_fact: Babies have about 300 separate bones; many fuse during growth, leaving adults with 206. The skull alone starts as several pieces joined by flexible cartilage.

questions.question: Roughly how much of your body weight is made up of bacteria and other microbes?
questions.fun_fact: You carry roughly the same number of microbial cells as human cells. Total mass is around 1–2 kg — most of it living in your gut, where it helps digest food and train immunity.

questions.question: Which organ in the human body can regrow itself even after most of it is removed?
questions.fun_fact: Remove up to 70% of a healthy liver and the remainder can grow back to nearly its original size within months — uniquely among major human organs.

questions.question: Why can't you tickle yourself?

answers.text: Your brain predicts the sensation and cancels it
Your skin's nerves shut down when you touch yourself
Tickling only works with cold fingers

questions.fun_fact: The cerebellum predicts the touch from your own hand and dampens the response. People with certain neurological conditions, like schizophrenia, can sometimes tickle themselves.

questions.question: Roughly how long would it take all the blood in your body to pass through your heart once?
questions.fun_fact: Your heart pumps about 5 litres per minute at rest — roughly your total blood volume. Every drop of you cycles through the heart roughly once a minute.

questions.question: What surprising thing happens to your height during the day?

answers.text: Your height stays exactly the same

questions.fun_fact: Gravity compresses the discs between your vertebrae over the day, so you measure shorter in the evening. A night's sleep lets the discs rehydrate and restore your height.

questions.question: Which sense is so 'wired up' to your brain that losing it can disrupt memory?
questions.fun_fact: Smell is the only sense routed directly to the limbic system, which handles memory and emotion. Loss of smell is sometimes an early warning of Alzheimer's or Parkinson's.

questions.question: What unusual thing did the early anaesthetic chloroform first become famous for?

answers.text: Queen Victoria using it during childbirth
Knocking out an elephant in a circus

questions.fun_fact: Chloroform was controversial because some believed pain in childbirth was 'natural'. Queen Victoria used it for the birth of Prince Leopold in 1853, making it socially acceptable.

questions.question: Which common procedure was once performed by barbers as a sideline to haircuts?

answers.text: Surgery — including tooth extractions and bloodletting

questions.fun_fact: Medieval barber-surgeons did everything from shaving to amputations. The red-and-white striped barber pole represents blood and bandages from those bloodletting days.

questions.question: What happens to GPS satellite clocks if you don't account for relativity?

answers.text: GPS positions would drift by about 10 km per day
Nothing — the effect is too small to matter

questions.fun_fact: GPS clocks tick faster than ground clocks by about 38 microseconds a day (gravitational + velocity effects combined). Engineers pre-tune the satellites' onboard clocks before launch so they appear correct from the ground.

questions.question: If you push an object hard enough, can it ever reach the speed of light?

answers.text: No — its mass effectively grows without bound

questions.fun_fact: As an object's speed approaches c, the energy needed to accelerate it further rises toward infinity. Only massless particles like photons travel at light speed — and they only ever travel at exactly that speed.

questions.question: What is unusual about the rest mass of a photon?

answers.text: It depends on the colour of the light
It is the same as an electron

questions.fun_fact: Photons have no rest mass — which is why they can travel at the speed of light. They still carry energy and momentum, which is how solar sails work.

questions.question: Which everyday object relies directly on quantum tunnelling to work?

answers.text: Flash memory in a USB stick

questions.fun_fact: Flash memory stores bits by trapping electrons that tunnel through a thin insulator. Without quantum tunnelling, USB sticks, SSDs, and modern smartphones couldn't store data.

questions.question: If you cool a gas, what happens to its entropy according to the third law of thermodynamics?

answers.text: It approaches a minimum as temperature approaches absolute zero
It stays constant regardless of temperature

questions.fun_fact: At absolute zero a perfect crystal would have zero entropy — only one possible microstate. Real materials always have some residual disorder, but they approach that limit asymptotically.

questions.question: Which fundamental particle is responsible for giving other particles mass?
questions.fun_fact: The Higgs field permeates all space. Particles interact with it to varying degrees — strong interactions yield heavy particles, no interaction yields massless ones like photons. CERN confirmed the Higgs in 2012.

questions.question: What happens to the perceived pitch of a siren as an ambulance speeds toward you?
questions.fun_fact: The Doppler effect compresses sound waves in front of a moving source and stretches them behind. The same effect on light tells astronomers whether galaxies are approaching (blueshift) or receding (redshift).

questions.question: Why does ice on a frozen lake feel slippery underfoot?

answers.text: A thin liquid-like layer forms on the surface even below freezing
Ice has a naturally frictionless crystal face
Pressure from your shoe melts the ice

questions.fun_fact: The old 'pressure melts the ice under your skates' story has been mostly debunked. Modern measurements show ice naturally has a quasi-liquid surface layer down to about -20°C — that's what makes it slippery.

questions.question: What surprising property does the element gallium have at body temperature?
questions.fun_fact: Gallium melts at about 29.8°C — below human body temperature. Magicians use it for the 'spoon that melts in your tea' trick because it stays solid at room temperature but liquefies on contact with warm skin.

questions.question: Which gas, despite making up roughly 78% of Earth's atmosphere, is mostly chemically inert at normal conditions?
questions.fun_fact: The triple bond in N2 is one of the strongest in chemistry — breaking it takes huge energy. That's why agriculture relies on the Haber-Bosch process, which uses high heat and pressure to fix atmospheric nitrogen into fertilizer.

questions.question: Pure gold is too soft for jewellery — what is typically added to harden it?
questions.fun_fact: 24-karat gold is so soft you can scratch it with a fingernail. Most jewellery is 18K or 14K — alloyed with copper (giving rose gold), silver (giving paler tones), or palladium (white gold) for durability.

questions.question: Why are diamonds and graphite so different despite both being pure carbon?

answers.text: Their carbon atoms are arranged in different crystal structures
Diamonds contain trace nitrogen, graphite doesn't
Graphite is a compound, not pure carbon

questions.fun_fact: Diamond's carbon atoms form a rigid 3D tetrahedral lattice (extremely hard). Graphite's atoms form weakly bonded sheets that slide past each other — which is why pencils write and graphite makes a good lubricant.

questions.question: Which everyday metal is the best electrical conductor of all elements?
questions.fun_fact: Silver beats copper slightly in conductivity, but copper is used for most wiring because it's far cheaper and doesn't tarnish in the same brittle way. Gold is used for connector plating because it never oxidises.

questions.question: What state of matter is a candle flame?

answers.text: Mostly gas, plus tiny incandescent particles

questions.fun_fact: Most candle flames aren't hot enough to ionise air into plasma. They're hot gas carrying glowing soot particles (incandescent carbon) that give the yellow colour. A much hotter blowtorch flame can reach plasma territory.

questions.question: How many chambers does a cow's stomach have?
questions.fun_fact: Cows are ruminants: the rumen, reticulum, omasum, and abomasum each play a role in breaking down tough plant fibres. Cows regurgitate and re-chew partially digested food as 'cud'.

questions.question: What is unusual about the DNA in your mitochondria?

answers.text: It is inherited only from your mother
It is identical to your father's

questions.fun_fact: Mitochondria carry their own circular DNA — a relic of an ancient bacterium that was absorbed by early cells. Sperm mitochondria are destroyed after fertilisation, so only the mother's are passed on.

questions.question: Roughly how many cells in the human body are replaced over a lifetime?

answers.text: Most cell types are continually replaced — but not neurons in the cortex
All cells are replaced every seven years
Cells are never replaced after childhood

questions.fun_fact: Gut lining cells turn over in days, skin cells in weeks, red blood cells in months, bone over years. But most neurons in your cerebral cortex were made before birth and stay with you for life.

questions.question: What does a tardigrade do when conditions become unbearable?

answers.text: It enters a near-dehydrated 'tun' state and can survive vacuum
It grows a hard shell and burrows underground

questions.fun_fact: Tardigrades (water bears) survive boiling, freezing, radiation, and even open space. They expel almost all water and curl into a 'tun' — metabolism nearly halts, and they rehydrate years later.

questions.question: How does an octopus 'see' colour despite being colourblind?

answers.text: It may sense colour through pigment-detecting cells in its skin
It memorises colours from chemical cues
Octopuses can't sense colour at all

questions.fun_fact: Octopus eyes have only one photoreceptor type — yet they perform vivid camouflage. One hypothesis: opsin proteins in their skin let the whole animal sample wavelength via a distributed 'skin-vision' system.

questions.question: Which sea creature is biologically considered effectively immortal under the right conditions?
questions.fun_fact: When stressed, Turritopsis dohrnii can revert from its adult medusa form back to a polyp and start its life cycle over. In the lab it has been observed doing this repeatedly — though predators still get most in the wild.

questions.question: Why do leaves change colour in autumn?

answers.text: Chlorophyll breaks down, revealing other pigments that were there all along
Leaves manufacture new red and yellow pigments in autumn
Falling temperatures bleach the leaves chemically

questions.fun_fact: Carotenoids (yellows/oranges) are present all summer but masked by green chlorophyll. As days shorten, trees recycle the chlorophyll and the underlying pigments become visible. Reds (anthocyanins) are often produced fresh in autumn.

questions.question: What surprising thing does your stomach lining do every few days?

answers.text: It rebuilds itself to avoid being digested by its own acid
It changes pH from acidic to alkaline
It absorbs most of the food you eat

questions.fun_fact: Stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve metal. A thick mucus layer protects the lining — and the cells underneath are replaced every few days, faster than nearly any other tissue.

questions.question: How do bees communicate the location of food to the hive?

answers.text: By performing a 'waggle dance' encoding angle and distance
By releasing a scented trail other bees follow
By guiding scouts back one at a time

questions.fun_fact: Karl von Frisch decoded the dance in the 1940s — the angle relative to vertical equals the angle to the food relative to the sun, and dance duration encodes distance. He won a Nobel Prize in 1973 for the discovery.

questions.question: Roughly how long does it take sunlight to reach Earth?
questions.fun_fact: Light travels 150 million kilometres from the Sun in about 8 minutes 20 seconds. The sunlight you see actually left the Sun's surface before you started reading this sentence.

questions.question: Which planet in our solar system has the fastest winds?
questions.fun_fact: Neptune's winds can exceed 2000 km/h — faster than the speed of sound on Earth. The cause is still debated, since Neptune receives barely any sunlight to drive weather.

questions.question: How many planets in our solar system could float in a sufficiently large body of water?

answers.text: One — Saturn, because it's less dense than water

questions.fun_fact: Saturn's average density is about 0.69 g/cm³ — lower than water (1 g/cm³). In a sufficiently large ocean it would float, though it would leave a colossal ring residue.

questions.question: Where in the solar system is the largest known canyon?
questions.fun_fact: Valles Marineris stretches over 4000 km across Mars — about as long as the United States is wide — and reaches 7 km deep in places. The Grand Canyon would be a side branch by comparison.

questions.question: What happens to a star roughly the size of our Sun at the end of its life?

answers.text: It sheds its outer layers and becomes a white dwarf
It collapses directly into a black hole

questions.fun_fact: Sun-sized stars expand into red giants, then puff off a glowing planetary nebula, leaving an Earth-sized white dwarf at the centre. Only stars roughly 8+ solar masses end as supernovae.

questions.question: Roughly how many stars are estimated to be in the observable universe?

answers.text: More than the grains of sand on all Earth's beaches
About the same as the world's population

questions.fun_fact: Astronomers estimate at least 10^22 stars in the observable universe — vastly more than the 10^18 or so grains of sand on Earth. Each large galaxy alone contains hundreds of billions of stars.

questions.question: What is unusual about Mercury's orbital path?

answers.text: Its orbit precesses — a tiny shift that confirmed general relativity
Its orbit is a perfect circle

questions.fun_fact: Mercury's perihelion shifts about 43 arcseconds per century beyond what Newtonian gravity predicts. Einstein's general relativity explained the gap exactly — one of its first observational confirmations in 1915.

questions.question: What is the cosmic microwave background?

answers.text: Leftover light from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang
Microwaves emitted by our own galaxy

questions.fun_fact: The CMB fills the universe in every direction at about 2.7 K. About 1% of the static on old analog TV sets tuned between channels was actually CMB photons that began their journey when the universe first became transparent.

questions.question: In a room of just 23 people, what is the probability that at least two share a birthday?
questions.fun_fact: The 'birthday paradox' is counterintuitive because we picture our own birthday matching someone, but the question is any pair matching — the number of possible pairs grows fast (23 people = 253 pairs).

questions.question: What is unusual about the number 1 when it comes to leading digits of real-world data?

answers.text: It appears as the leading digit about 30% of the time
It almost never appears as a leading digit
It appears with exactly 11% frequency, like every other digit

questions.fun_fact: Benford's Law: in many datasets — populations, financial figures, physical constants — leading digits follow a logarithmic distribution where 1 appears ~30%, 2 ~17%, down to 9 ~5%. Auditors use it to detect fraud.

questions.question: If you fold a sheet of paper in half 42 times, roughly how thick would it be?

answers.text: Thick enough to reach the Moon
About the height of a skyscraper

questions.fun_fact: Doubling 42 times multiplies thickness by 2^42 ≈ 4.4 trillion. A 0.1 mm sheet becomes around 440,000 km thick — beyond lunar distance. In practice, paper can usually only be folded 7–8 times before it becomes unfoldable.

questions.question: How many holes does a standard drinking straw have?

answers.text: One — topologically it's a single tube
Zero — both ends are openings, not holes

questions.fun_fact: Topologists count by genus — the number of 'handles' on a surface. A straw is topologically equivalent to a donut (torus), which has one hole. A coffee mug also has exactly one — the handle.

questions.question: Why does your nose run when you eat very spicy food?

answers.text: Capsaicin triggers nerves that signal irritation, prompting mucus production
Spice molecules physically push mucus out
Stomach acid rises and reaches the nose

questions.fun_fact: Capsaicin binds to TRPV1 receptors — the same nerves that detect physical heat and damage. Your brain reads it as a burn, and reflexes like runny nose and sweating kick in to 'cool' the perceived injury.

questions.question: Roughly how much blood does an average adult human contain?
questions.fun_fact: Average adults carry about 4.5–5.5 litres of blood, roughly 7% of body weight. Blood plasma alone is about 90% water — which is why staying hydrated keeps circulation efficient.

questions.question: Which type of vaccine introduced the very first inoculation against a disease?

answers.text: A smallpox vaccine using cowpox material

questions.fun_fact: In 1796 Edward Jenner inoculated a boy with cowpox material and showed it protected against smallpox. The Latin word for cow ('vacca') gave us 'vaccine'. Smallpox is the only human disease eradicated worldwide.

questions.question: Why don't your eyes get tired even though they move constantly all day?

answers.text: Eye muscles are the fastest and most efficient in the body
Your eyes barely move when you focus
Eyes use ATP recycled from blinking

questions.fun_fact: Eye muscles can make over 100,000 movements daily and rarely fatigue. They have very high mitochondrial density and fast-twitch fibres optimised for tiny, precise corrections — your eyes never sit perfectly still even when 'fixed' on a point.

questions.question: What unusual thing happens to your blood vessels when you blush?

answers.text: Facial veins dilate in response to a social-emotion signal
Blood vessels constrict to push blood to the face

questions.fun_fact: Blushing is unique in that it's a vascular reaction to emotion alone — no other species shows the same conscious flush. Darwin called it 'the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions'.

questions.question: What did the word 'bug' in computing originally refer to?

answers.text: An actual moth found inside a 1947 relay computer
Confused code by an early programmer
A misreading of a binary instruction

questions.fun_fact: Grace Hopper's team taped a moth into the Harvard Mark II's logbook in 1947, noting 'first actual case of bug being found'. The metaphor of 'bugs' for technical faults already existed — but this cemented the term in computing.

questions.question: Who is generally credited as the first computer programmer?
questions.fun_fact: In the 1840s Ada Lovelace wrote an algorithm for Charles Babbage's never-built Analytical Engine — to compute Bernoulli numbers. She also speculated machines could one day compose music, anticipating general-purpose computing.

questions.question: What was Alan Turing's famous proposed test for machine intelligence originally called?
questions.fun_fact: In his 1950 paper Turing proposed an 'imitation game' where a judge chats with a human and a machine via text and must tell them apart. The term 'Turing Test' came later from other researchers.

questions.question: Roughly how often has the number of transistors on a chip doubled, as observed by Gordon Moore?
questions.fun_fact: Moore's 1965 observation projected a doubling roughly every year, later revised to about every two years. It guided the chip industry for decades — though physical limits are now slowing the pace.

questions.question: What original purpose did the @ symbol serve before email made it famous?

answers.text: It meant 'at the rate of' in accounting and trade
It was invented for email and had no prior use
It marked footnotes in medieval manuscripts

questions.fun_fact: The @ symbol meant 'at the price of' for centuries (e.g. '5 apples @ 10 cents'). Ray Tomlinson picked it in 1971 to separate user from machine in early email because it was unambiguous and unused in names.

questions.question: Which sweetener was discovered when a researcher licked his finger after handling chemicals in the lab?
questions.fun_fact: James Schlatter discovered aspartame in 1965 while developing an ulcer drug. He licked his finger to pick up paper, tasted intense sweetness, and traced it to the intermediate compound — now in thousands of diet products.

questions.question: How was X-ray imaging first discovered?

answers.text: Wilhelm Röntgen noticed a fluorescent screen glowing across the room
Marie Curie isolated them from uranium ore

questions.fun_fact: In 1895 Röntgen was experimenting with cathode-ray tubes when he saw a barium-coated screen fluoresce despite being shielded. Weeks later he produced the first X-ray image — of his wife's hand and wedding ring.

questions.question: Vulcanised rubber was invented after Charles Goodyear accidentally did what?

answers.text: Dropped a rubber-sulphur mix onto a hot stove
Buried rubber in a sulphur mine

questions.fun_fact: Goodyear had been trying for years to stop natural rubber from melting in summer and cracking in winter. The 1839 stove accident showed sulphur + heat created a tough, elastic material — modern tyres descend from that mishap.

questions.question: What surprising property does graphene — a single layer of carbon atoms — have?

answers.text: It's stronger than steel by weight, yet flexible and conductive

questions.fun_fact: A single sheet of graphene is about 200 times stronger than steel of the same thickness. Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov isolated it in 2004 using sticky tape on graphite — and won the 2010 Nobel Prize.

questions.question: How does an electric eel actually generate its shock?

answers.text: Specialised cells stacked like batteries fire simultaneously
Friction from rapid swimming generates current
It absorbs static electricity from the water

questions.fun_fact: Electrocytes — modified muscle cells — line the eel's body. When fired in unison they produce pulses up to 600 volts. The same principle inspired Alessandro Volta's first battery design in 1800.

questions.question: Why does cracking your knuckles make a popping sound?

answers.text: Gas bubbles in joint fluid rapidly form or collapse
Bones briefly grind against each other

questions.fun_fact: Synovial fluid contains dissolved gases. Stretching the joint drops the pressure and forms a tiny cavity — the pop is the cavity collapsing or forming. Long-running studies show knuckle cracking does NOT cause arthritis.
